summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that the offence covers sodomy and acts involving contact between males that a reasonable person would regard as indecent. Sodomy is classified in the Criminal Code as unlawful sexual conduct, defined as anal sexual intercourse or any indecent act between consenting adults, with common-law formulations covering "unlawful and intentional sexual relations per anum between two human males" and "unnatural offences".

A 2006 revision of the Criminal Code expanded sodomy beyond sexual activity to any act involving contact between two males that a reasonable person would regard as an indecent act, and added a sexual deviancy offence covering holding hands, hugging or kissing between two people of the same sex. That amendment was one of fifteen additions made to the Criminal Code in 2006.

Gender marker change is not allowed. Section 18(2) of the Births and Deaths Registration Act permits a first-name change only on application to the Registrar General with evidence justifying the need, and the Registrar General's discretion may defeat a change sought on grounds of gender identity. Activist Jordan Chanetsa is documented as commenting that transgender people face difficulty accessing legal work because official documents do not reflect their gender.

Bathroom use carries a documented arrest risk. In 2014 trans activist Rikki Nathanson was arrested on a criminal nuisance charge for using a women's bathroom; the charge was thrown out, she sued for damages and won, and in 2015 she established Trans Research, Education, Advocacy & Training (TREAT). The 2014 arrest is the most recent trans-specific incident documented in this record, and no later instance is documented.

Public health facilities operate under a stated duty to serve trans patients. In July 2018 the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender and non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, and that nowhere in policy or law is it illegal to provide healthcare services to members of these groups; it was issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. Health ministry training manuals further require health professionals to support the unique healthcare needs of transgender and non-gender-conforming people, and state that the criminalisation of sex work, drug use and some sexual acts creates disproportionate harms, undermines HIV prevention for the whole nation and impairs access to healthcare. Formal policy therefore guarantees health-service access at public facilities, while day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under the 2018 handbook.

Same-sex marriage is banned by the Constitution, which was amended in 2013 to define marriage as between a man and a woman, and in May 2019 Cabinet approved marriage-law amendments to align the ban. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no route to recognition in Zimbabwe.

LGBTQ people have no general legal protections from discrimination, violence and harassment. The two exceptions are protection of sexual-orientation-based personal information under the Freedom of Information Act (2020) and the Cyber and Data Protection Act (2022).

Since 1995 the Government has carried out campaigns against homosexual men and women, with enforcement including infiltration of GALZ, bribery, detention, beating, killing and rape by authorities, and reported use of the Central Intelligence Organisation to beat and arrest homosexuals. Section 11 of the Censorship and Entertainments Control Act, which prohibits undesirable publications defined as indecent or obscene or offensive or harmful to public morals or likely to be contrary to public health, has been used to harass LGBTQ people and activists.

Prosecution under the sodomy provisions has reached the highest office. In 1998 former President Canaan Banana was found guilty on eleven charges of sodomy, attempted sodomy and indecent assault after a 1996 arrest, sentenced to 10 years imprisonment, defrocked, and served 6 months in an open prison.

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990 with more than 4,000 community members, 10 affinity groups, 4 resource centres and 35 years of advocacy, provides legal support explicitly covering arrests for sodomy, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. Legal aid and counselling remain reachable for an LGBTI traveller despite criminalisation.
tangentialFactors:
Amnesty International report of 9 January 2024, index AFR 01/7533/2024, titled "We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries", examines anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people across several countries in one region. The inventory does not state whether Zimbabwe is among the countries examined, so the report is carried as regional context rather than as a finding on Zimbabwe.

No comparative or ranking data is available in this inventory. There are no per-capita figures, incident counts by jurisdiction or sentencing statistics, so no assessment of Zimbabwe's position relative to other countries can be made from these sources.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the penalties or sentencing ranges attached to sodomy, indecent contact or the sexual deviancy offence, so no exposure figure can be given.

Current enforcement frequency is not sourced. The record documents the 1998 conviction of former President Canaan Banana on eleven sodomy, attempted sodomy and indecent assault charges after a 1996 arrest, and the 2014 arrest of Rikki Nathanson, but no prosecution counts, periods or rates are available.

Whether the July 2018 health ministry handbook remains in force, and how many practitioners have been trained under it, is unresolved in these sources. The same applies to whether the marriage-law amendments Cabinet approved in May 2019 were enacted.

No information is sourced on entry rules, visa conditions, border document checks or screening of gender presentation at ports of entry, and no trans-specific violence statistics with a denominator, a period or a comparison to the general homicide rate appear in the inventory. The date of the damages award in the 2014 bathroom case is not specified.
